https://www.dw.com/en/us-imposes-new-san.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J2gv Russia is the only other country to sanction ICC President Akane [FILE: November 20, 2024] Image: Eva Plevier/ANP/AFP Advertisement US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday announced that the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and a senior trial lawyer. The move is the latest escalation in the Trump administration's attacks on the international body. Established in 2002 and based in The Hague, Netherlands, the ICC prosecutes war crimes , genocide and crimes against humanity. The US is not a member of the Court. What did Rubio say about the sanctions against the ICC? Rubio said the US — acting under authority of an executive order signed by President Donald Trump — had leveled sanctions against ICC President Tomoko Akane, a Japanese judge; and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the ICC. "These individuals," said Rubio, "have directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC ‌jurisdiction." Rubio wrote Tuesday on X that the move was part of Washington's "unwavering mission to protect Americans from this sham of a court." Why is the US trying to undermine the ICC? The ICC asserts its jurisdiction only if member states are unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities themselves. However, the Court's statute also gives it the power to prosecute nationals of non-member states who commit atrocities on the territory of a member state. Rubio argues the ICC poses a threat to US personnel carrying out President Trump's hardline immigration policies or "drug interdiction" strikes on boats in international waters, as well as other US ⁠service members. "The Trump Administration has been clear: The International Criminal Court is a corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate," the State Department said in a statement . "We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty." US takes aim at the International Criminal Court To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Last year, the US imposed sanctions on several ICC officials after the Court issued arrest warrants for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Yoav Galant over the war in Gaza. Last month, Rubio said the Trump administration would step up its efforts to undermine the ICC, including a diplomatic campaign aimed ​at persuading other countries to ‌quit the Court. Chad and Venezuela, for instance, have already heeded the US call and withdrawn from the ICC. Trump has said the US campaign is aimed at defending ally Netanyahu and others from prosecution, not himself. Three ICC judges sued the Trump administration in June, calling sanctions illegal; and last week, four human rights groups followed suit, arguing that victims of war crimes were being denied justice as a result of the president's actions. How has the ICC reacted to Washington's latest attack? Tuesday's sanctions bar Akane and Seye from entering the US and from making transactions within the US financial system. The ICC on Tuesday said it remains "undeterred" and stands behind all its staff. The Court rejected Washington's approach, saying "measures targeting judges, prosecutors and staff who work towards the fulfillment of the mandate that was conferred to the ICC by states undermine the rule of law." "When judicial actors are threatened for applying the law, it is the international legal order itself that is placed at risk," the Court said in a statement. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-rusting-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J2VN Removing old munitions from German waters is a massive task that will require increased resources and likely take decades Image: Jana Ulrich/Forschungstauchzentrum CAU Kiel/dpa//picture alliance Advertisement Beneath the seas off Germany's northern coast, vast quantities of bombs and other weapons are slowly rusting away. They are part of an estimated 1.6 million metric tons of conventional munitions in the North Sea and Baltic Sea , a legacy of two world wars and the mass disposal of weapons after 1945. How old weapons pose a new threat For decades, the material was largely left alone unless it posed an explosive danger. But as metal casings corrode, a different problem is emerging. Some weapons are remnants of fighting: mines, unexploded bombs and ammunition lost at sea. But huge quantities were deliberately dumped after Nazi Germany surrendered in 1945, as the Allies disposed of the country's vast arsenal. What was once regarded as an explosive hazard has now become an environmental one. "It's clear that due to corrosion of these items, compounds enter the marine ecosystem and enter marine life," Kiel University toxicologist Edmund Maser told DW. "It turned out that these compounds are toxic and carcinogenic, both for human life and also for marine life," he said. Among the most toxic compounds in the old weapons is trinitrotoluene, or TNT, a military explosive. Jörn Scharsack of Germany's Thünen Institute of Fisheries Ecology looked for evidence of it in dab fish. Simply detonating the munitions underwater is not considered an ideal solution as the blast waves can harm marine life and release toxic residues Image: Carsten Rehder/dpa/picture alliance "We find TNT in the fish, or let's say, metabolization, degradation products of TNT," he said. The quantities are tiny — measured in nanograms — and not every fish contains detectable levels. But researchers repeatedly find the compounds around old munitions hotspots. "It's low. But it's there." How toxic munitions are affecting marine life So far, the contamination does not appear to be making fish acutely sick. "The fish look healthy when we take them out. They do not have more diseases in terms of viral, bacterial, parasite diseases," Scharsack told DW. There is, however, one recurring abnormal finding. "What we see is tumors, so tumors in the liver. That pops up again and again." Maser's group has also found munitions compounds in fish, as well as mussels. Together with the Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI) in Bremerhaven, his team found liver abnormalities in more than 50% of fish living around some munitions dumping grounds and wrecks, compared with normal rates of just 1–2%. Mussels, meanwhile, showed biochemical signs of oxidative stress. As TNT is metabolized, highly reactive forms of oxygen can damage proteins, lipids and even DNA. "This can be a step towards cancer," said Maser. And the contamination does not stop with fish and mussels. Maser's team has also detected TNT-related compounds in tissue samples from two stranded whales , showing that the chemicals are reaching animals at the top of the marine food web. "That means that these compounds have arrived in top predators," he said. Are Germany's sea munitions dangerous to humans? That raises the obvious question: If TNT-related compounds are reaching top predators, are people who eat seafood at risk? For now, both scientists say the answer is no. Whales face more constant exposure through prey and surrounding water, while humans are exposed only occasionally through seafood. "One would need to eat lots of fish to really reach a level where it's getting dangerous," said Scharsack. "I'm still going swimming. I'm still eating fish." The concern is what happens as the munitions continue to deteriorate. "I would say it's likely to get worse if we look at the ongoing corrosion of the munitions," Scharsack said. Baltic sea: poison and grenades To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "The shells are corroding. More and more of the toxic substances are lying open, exposed to the water." The problem appears worse in the Baltic than the North Sea because weaker currents and water exchange allow leaking pollutants to linger rather than disperse. What mussels reveal about TNT contamination Maser's research suggests this may already be happening. His team examined archived mussels dating back to 1985 and found TNT-related contamination increasing steadily from around 2000 through 2022. "It's low, but it's increasing," he said. "And we expect that over the coming decades, maybe two or three or four decades, we will have concentrations that could maybe harm the human seafood consumer." Marine life is already under pressure from what Maser described as a "whole cocktail" of human-made pollutants, including microplastics , pesticides and pharmaceutical compounds. Munitions add another contaminant to that mix. Unlike many of those pollutants, which are already dispersed through the oceans, bombs and mines remain physical objects that can be salvaged and disposed of. And the window will not stay open forever. Germany has long removed munitions posing an immediate danger, but only recently began pilot projects for systematic clearance to prevent environmental harm . "The topic has been ignored for decades. Nobody wanted to talk about it," Scharsack said. What are the challenges in clearing munitions? In a study published in July, GEOMAR researcher Torsten Frey and colleagues identified 484 known or potential munitions piles in two areas of the Baltic Sea. But of the estimated 1.6 million tons of munitions in German waters, around 1.5 million tons have yet to be mapped, Frey told DW. In the past, bombs have often been removed and disposed of on land, but that is set to change Image: Christian Charisius/dpa/picture alliance Recovering the munitions from known locations is no longer the main obstacle, Frey said, with specialist companies able to clear large quantities relatively quickly. "The bottleneck is the disposal and destruction of the recovered munitions." Germany is developing an offshore treatment platform to help increase disposal capacity. "This will be a marathon, not a sprint," said Frey. Even clearance will leave small pieces of explosive behind, some no larger than "a sugar cube." Maser is investigating whether marine bacteria and fungi could eventually break down these residues into CO2 and water. The work is still at the laboratory stage and Maser stresses that it cannot replace physical clearance. "We need more of these platforms," he said. "We need to start as early as possible." "If we wait maybe 40 years, then maybe all these metal cases are corroded and we have then no chance to get these munition compounds out of the water," said Maser. "This is why we should act now." Photo Credit: Kremlin.ru Opinion 1 Europe Social Issues September 21, 2026 September 21, 2026 Paul Goble 0 Comments By Paul Goble Key Takeaways: Wrong lens. Temaglavnoe.ru says Western handicapping of Putin’s heir treats Russia like other countries’ job boards. The portal’s claim: the state is a living system that will surface whoever can speak for its “current historical cycle,” not whoever is pre-appointed. Eight misses it lists. Informal debts and school/service ties; historical memory and “cultural codes”; chance and chaos; ideology (a bare technocrat cannot hold elites); regions and society, not only Moscow; siloviki as rivals, not one bloc; business as fragments, not a chamber; the “prince” myth—status lasts only while the father is useful; power is not inherited. What it says the system wants. In a personalist transit, the prize is not a title but a balancer who can keep competing corporations even and still impose a will. Without that, turbulence—which almost everyone at the top wants to dodge. . Western analysts constantly propose possible successors to Vladimir Putin and even seek to handicap them in much the same way they do possible future leaders in other countries, the Important Theme portal says; but in adopting that approach, they almost invariably miss “the main thing.” These analysts and commentators “do not see that the Russian government is no the sum of positions but a living system that during transit finds as its leader not someone who will be appointed but rather someone who can be the expression of the objective interests of the state in its current historical cycle” ( temaglavnoe.ru/russia/32272/ ). By employing for Russia the optic they use in analyzing political transition in other countries, the portal’s authors continue, they “lose sight of the deep tectonic processes that determine the real architecture of the Russian state, the political culture of the state, its historical experience and the mentality of its people.” The portal’s authors list eight failngs of Western analyses of the upcoming transition in Russia in this regard: First, these analysts “do not see the role of informal networks and personal relationships” that are so critical in Russia … invisible threads of personal obligation, long-standing friendships, joint experiences of study or service and unspoken arrangements, all of which are often more important” than any superficial set of views and responsibilities. Second, these analysts “ignore historical memory and cultural codes … The figure of the successor there should not just be ‘fit into parameters;,’ it must resonate with the deep expectations of the elites and society.” Third, Western analysts “do not take into account the factor of randomness and unpredictability,” critical because “the transfer of power iw not a planned operation but often a chaotic process in which unforeseen circumstances play a decisive role” and mistakes in the course of this can transfer a frontrunner to an also ran very quickly. Fourth, such analysts typically “overlook the role of ideology and values” and thus they don’t recognize that “a technocrat without an ideological agenda won’t be able to consolidate elites at this time of crisis.” Fifth, these analysts “ignore the regional factor and the diversity of Russia.” Russia is far more than Moscow however little attention Western analysts give to Russai outside of Moscow. More generally, they ignore society, a mistake because “even in an authoritariansystem, popular legitimacy is important.” Sixth, most Western analysts treat the security services as a monolithic whole and do not understand the tensions among its component parts. Those aren’t always visible in public but they are always present and in a succession crisis, each will want the best for itself. Seventh, most of these analysts make the same mistake about the business community. It too is fragmented rather than being a unified whole and won’t act the way these analysts appear to think. And eighth, these analysts generally accept “the myth” of the Russian “princes,” forgetting that “in Russia the status of ‘prince’ exists only as long as their fathers are a resource and that “power isn’t inherited. And lying behind all of these errors is another fundamental one: “In personalist regimes, the transit of power is not so much a struggle for this or that position but a search for a figure capable of maintain and intra-elite balance.” Without that, there will be turbulence, something almost all of those involved want to avoid. When the looming transition occurs, the portal says, “at the top of the power will be not the one who simply ‘agree’ with the clans and not the richest ‘businessman.’ Instead, the system will put forward someone who can ensure a tight balance of interests by becoming a figure acceptable to competing corporations — and also able to impose his will on that balance.” About Paul Goble Paul Goble is a longtime specialist on ethnic and religious questions in Eurasia. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/victor-p.text: Victor Ponta urges Nicușor Dan not to miss the Saudi Arabia Summit Former Prime Minister Victor Ponta is urging President Nicușor Dan to attend the summit between the European Union and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), scheduled for October 24 in Saudi Arabia. Ponta argues that the visit would mark a historic first for Romania and offer an opportunity to revitalize economic relations with states in the region, at a time when Saudi Arabia is facing a series of missile and drone attacks. On Tuesday, Victor Ponta issued a public message to President Nicușor Dan, urging him to accept the invitation to attend the EU-GCC summit alongside European leaders and representatives of the six Gulf monarchies. The former prime minister believes Romania should not miss such a gathering, considering both its economic interests and its diplomatic positioning amidst Middle East tensions. „The Romanian saying ‘God builds a nest for the one-eyed stork’ still holds true!” Victor Ponta began in the message posted on Facebook. „The invitation extended to the President of Romania—alongside the other 26 heads of state and government—to attend the EU-GCC Summit is a historic opportunity for Romania, one I hope we do not miss!” the former prime minister continued. Ponta: It Would Be the First Visit by a Romanian President to Saudi Arabia Victor Ponta presents four arguments in favor of Nicușor Dan attending the international meeting. First of all, the former prime minister argues that the trip would mark the first visit by a Romanian president to Saudi Arabia, a country with major geopolitical and economic influence. „I visited there as prime minister, but no Romanian president has ever been to Riyadh,” Ponta states. He also points out that the Romanian president would have the opportunity to hold direct talks with the leaders of all six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Oman. Another argument raised by the former prime minister concerns the security situation in the region. „This is a crucial moment for Romania to demonstrate solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the face of the terrorist attacks it is currently enduring,” Victor Ponta wrote. Finally, the former head of government maintains that attending the summit could help revive economic projects discussed during his 2015 official visit—projects he claims have been „frozen” for the past 11 years. „I hope President Nicușor Dan decides to attend! God willing! Inshallah!” Victor Ponta concluded his message. EU-GCC Summit Scheduled for October 24 The meeting Victor Ponta refers to will take place on October 24, 2026, in Saudi Arabia, and will mark the second high-level summit between the European Union and the Gulf Cooperation Council. According to the official announcement by the European Council, the meeting will be co-chaired on the European side by António Costa, President of the European Council, with the European Union also represented by Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission. The first EU–GCC summit took place in Brussels in October 2024, focusing on strengthening the strategic partnership between the two regions. The cooperation agenda covers trade, investment, energy, climate change, and regional security, including diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia hit by deadly attacks ahead of the meeting The summit comes at a particularly tense time for Saudi Arabia, following attacks launched against King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On October 10, 12 people were killed and over 300 injured in an attack attributed to Iran-backed Houthi rebels from Yemen. The airport was targeted again in the following days, causing further casualties and major air traffic disruptions. The attacks have heightened fears of the regional conflict spreading and raised questions regarding the ability of Saudi air defense systems to protect strategic infrastructure.
